notes.front: What is the difference between a stateful and a stateless app?
notes.back: A stateful app must store data (state) to work as designed; a stateless app handles each request independently, remembering nothing.
notes.explanation: Cloud native apps are scaled, restarted and moved around, so stateful apps need storage they can reach from anywhere.
notes.example: An online shop that remembers your basket is stateful; a search engine that forgets your search once you close the window is stateless.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary, “Stateful Apps” and “Stateless Apps”

notes.front: What is a volume in Kubernetes?
notes.back: A directory, possibly holding data, that the containers in a Pod can access.
notes.explanation: Files written inside a container are lost when it crashes; a volume keeps data across container restarts and lets containers in a Pod share files.
notes.example: A web-server container and a content-fetching container in one Pod both mount the same volume, one writing files, the other serving them.

notes.front: What is an emptyDir volume?
notes.back: A volume that starts empty when the Pod is assigned to a node and is deleted permanently when the Pod leaves that node.
notes.explanation: All containers in the Pod can read and write it, which makes it ideal scratch space. It survives container crashes, because a crash does not remove the Pod.
notes.example: Scratch space for a disk-based merge sort.

notes.front: What is an ephemeral volume?
notes.back: A volume whose lifetime is tied to one Pod: it is created and deleted along with the Pod.
notes.explanation: Persistent volumes, by contrast, exist beyond the life of any individual Pod, and Kubernetes does not destroy them when the Pod goes.
notes.example: A cache that can be rebuilt, or read-only configuration files injected into a Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Ephemeral Volumes”; Kubernetes documentation, “Volumes”, “How volumes work”

notes.front: What is a PersistentVolume (PV)?
notes.back: A piece of storage in the cluster, provisioned by an administrator or dynamically, whose lifecycle is independent of any Pod.
notes.explanation: The PV API hides how storage is provided (network file shares, network disks or a cloud disk) from how it is consumed. A PV is a cluster resource, like a node.
notes.example: A 100 GiB cloud disk represented in the cluster as a PV object, waiting to be claimed.

notes.front: What is a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)?
notes.back: A user’s request for storage, stating size and access mode, which binds to a PersistentVolume that the Pod then mounts as a volume.
notes.explanation: PVCs consume PV resources the way Pods consume node resources; users ask for storage without knowing how it is implemented.
notes.example: A claim for 10 GiB of read-write storage, mounted by a database Pod at /var/lib/data.

notes.front: What is a StorageClass?
notes.back: An object that lets administrators describe the kinds of storage on offer, with the provisioner and parameters used to create volumes of that kind.
notes.explanation: The provisioner is the code that creates the storage. Classes can map to quality-of-service levels or backup policies; users request one by name in their claim.
notes.example: Classes named “fast” (SSD) and “slow” (standard disk); a PVC asks for storageClassName: fast.

notes.front: What is dynamic volume provisioning?
notes.back: Creating storage volumes automatically when users create PersistentVolumeClaims, instead of administrators pre-creating them.
notes.explanation: It is based on StorageClass objects, each naming a provisioner (the code that creates the storage) and the parameters to pass to it.
notes.example: A developer creates a PVC for class “fast”; the cloud disk and its PV appear within seconds, with no ticket to the admin team.

notes.front: What are a PersistentVolume’s access modes?
notes.back: Settings describing how a volume can be mounted: read-write or read-only, and by one node, many nodes or one Pod.
notes.explanation: Each PV lists the modes its storage supports, and Kubernetes uses them to match claims to volumes.
notes.example: An NFS share can support many read-write clients; a single cloud disk may support only one node at a time.

notes.front: What is a PersistentVolume’s reclaim policy?
notes.back: The rule telling the cluster what to do with the volume once its claim is deleted: keep it, delete it, or (deprecated) scrub it.
notes.explanation: It decides whether data survives when a user deletes their PVC.
notes.example: A PV with policy Retain keeps its data after the claim is removed, so an admin can recover it.

notes.front: What is a volume plugin?
notes.back: Code that lets Kubernetes attach and mount a type of storage for Pods. In-tree plugins ship with Kubernetes; out-of-tree plugins are developed separately.
notes.explanation: StorageClasses name a volume plugin (a provisioner) to create volumes dynamically.
notes.example: A plugin that knows how to attach a particular cloud provider’s disks to nodes.

notes.front: What is the Container Storage Interface (CSI)?
notes.back: A standard interface for exposing storage systems to containers, so vendors can write out-of-tree storage plugins for Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: Vendors no longer need to add code to the Kubernetes repository; you deploy their CSI driver, then create a StorageClass that uses it.
notes.example: A storage vendor ships a CSI driver; the cluster admin installs it and defines a StorageClass pointing at it.

notes.front: What is FlexVolume?
notes.back: A deprecated interface for out-of-tree volume plugins, whose driver binaries must be installed on each host with root access.
notes.explanation: CSI addresses FlexVolume’s limitations, and the storage community recommends writing a CSI driver instead.
notes.example: An old in-house storage driver installed as a binary on every node, which should be replaced by a CSI driver.

notes.front: What is a hostPath volume?
notes.back: A volume that mounts a file or directory from the host node’s filesystem into a Pod.
notes.explanation: Most Pods never need it, and the docs warn that it “presents many security risks”; it is a powerful escape hatch for a few applications.
notes.example: A node agent reading the node’s log directory /var/log through a hostPath mount.

notes.front: What is a projected volume?
notes.back: A volume that maps several existing volume sources, such as a Secret, a ConfigMap and downward API data, into one directory.
notes.explanation: All the sources must be in the same namespace as the Pod.
notes.example: One /etc/app directory holding a Secret’s password file and a ConfigMap’s settings file side by side.

notes.front: What is a VolumeSnapshot?
notes.back: A user’s request for a snapshot of a volume on a storage system, much as a PVC is a request for storage.
notes.explanation: The snapshot itself is a VolumeSnapshotContent (like a PV), and a VolumeSnapshotClass holds its attributes (like a StorageClass).
notes.example: Snapshotting a database’s PVC before an upgrade, so a new PVC can be restored from it if needed.

notes.front: What is cloud native storage?
notes.back: Storage technology built for containerised applications on platforms such as Kubernetes, serving mainly stateful apps.
notes.explanation: Traditional storage often struggles to scale and connect with modern apps; cloud native storage is designed for dynamic environments.
notes.example: A storage system that provisions a volume automatically whenever a new database Pod asks for one.

notes.front: Kubernetes can automatically mount a storage system of your choice, such as local storage or a public cloud provider’s. Which capability is this?
notes.back: Storage orchestration.
notes.explanation: You choose the storage system; Kubernetes mounts it for you.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Overview”, “Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do”

notes.front: If a container in a Pod restarts, what happens to data in the Pod’s volumes?
notes.back: It is kept: for every kind of volume, data is preserved across container restarts.
notes.explanation: Without a volume, the kubelet restarts a crashed container with a clean filesystem and its files are lost.

notes.front: How many volume types can one Pod use at the same time?
notes.back: Any number.
notes.explanation: Volumes are listed in .spec.volumes and mounted per container with volumeMounts, each at its own path.

notes.front: Does data in an emptyDir volume survive a container crash?
notes.back: Yes. A crash does not remove the Pod from the node; the data is lost only when the Pod is removed.
notes.explanation: emptyDir data is deleted permanently when the Pod leaves the node for any reason.

notes.front: What happens when an emptyDir volume sets medium: "Memory"?
notes.back: Kubernetes mounts a RAM-backed tmpfs; it is very fast, but files written count against the container’s memory limit.
notes.explanation: By default emptyDir uses whatever medium backs the node, such as disk, SSD or network storage.

notes.front: Besides emptyDir, which kinds of ephemeral volume inject Kubernetes data into a Pod?
notes.back: configMap, secret and downwardAPI volumes (an image volume can also mount container image files).
notes.explanation: Ephemeral volumes are declared inline in the Pod spec and are created and deleted with the Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Ephemeral Volumes”, “Types of ephemeral volumes”

notes.front: What are the two ways PersistentVolumes can be provisioned?
notes.back: Statically, by an administrator creating them in advance, or dynamically, through a StorageClass when a claim needs one.
notes.explanation: Dynamic provisioning happens when no static PV matches a claim and the claim requests a storage class configured for it.

notes.front: How many PersistentVolumeClaims can be bound to one PersistentVolume at a time?
notes.back: One: PVC-to-PV binding is an exclusive one-to-one mapping.
notes.explanation: A control loop in the control plane matches new claims to PVs; once bound, the binding is exclusive however it was made.

notes.front: What happens to a PersistentVolumeClaim if no matching volume exists?
notes.back: It stays unbound indefinitely, and binds as soon as a matching volume becomes available.
notes.explanation: The user always gets at least what was asked for; the bound volume may be larger than requested.

notes.front: Which three fields does every StorageClass contain for dynamic provisioning?
notes.back: provisioner, parameters and reclaimPolicy.
notes.explanation: They say which volume plugin creates the volume, what options it gets, and what happens to the volume after release.

notes.front: A PersistentVolumeClaim names no storageClassName. Which class does it use?
notes.back: The cluster’s default StorageClass, if one is marked as default.
notes.explanation: If there is no default, the claim’s class stays unset until one becomes available. A claim requesting class "" opts out of dynamic provisioning.

notes.front: What must a cluster administrator create before dynamic provisioning can happen?
notes.back: One or more StorageClass objects.
notes.explanation: Each StorageClass names the provisioner and parameters used when a claim asks for that class.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Dynamic Volume Provisioning”, “Enabling Dynamic Provisioning”

notes.front: What does the ReadWriteOnce (RWO) access mode allow?
notes.back: Read-write mounting by a single node; several Pods on that same node can still use it.
notes.explanation: For access by exactly one Pod, use ReadWriteOncePod instead.

notes.front: What does the ReadOnlyMany (ROX) access mode allow?
notes.back: Read-only mounting by many nodes.
notes.explanation: Useful for shared data that many Pods read but none change.

notes.front: What does the ReadWriteMany (RWX) access mode allow?
notes.back: Read-write mounting by many nodes.
notes.explanation: Only some storage supports it; NFS, for example, can support multiple read-write clients.

notes.front: What does the ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) access mode allow, and what does it require?
notes.back: Read-write mounting by a single Pod in the whole cluster. It works only with CSI volumes.
notes.explanation: It has been stable since v1.29.

notes.front: A volume supports several access modes. How many can it be mounted with at once?
notes.back: One: a volume is mounted using one access mode at a time.
notes.explanation: Also, apart from ReadWriteOncePod, access modes do not enforce write protection once mounted; they are used to match claims and volumes.

notes.front: Under the Retain reclaim policy, what happens to a PersistentVolume when its claim is deleted?
notes.back: The PV remains, marked “released”, with the old data still on it; an administrator must reclaim it manually.
notes.explanation: It is not available for another claim until the admin deletes it, cleans the data and, if wanted, recreates it.

notes.front: Under the Delete reclaim policy, what is removed when the claim is released?
notes.back: Both the PersistentVolume object and the storage asset behind it in the external infrastructure.
notes.explanation: Dynamically provisioned volumes inherit their StorageClass’s reclaim policy, which defaults to Delete.

notes.front: A dynamically provisioned volume takes its reclaim policy from its StorageClass, where the default is {{c1::Delete}}.
notes.explanation: Administrators should set the class’s policy to match users’ expectations, or patch each PV afterwards.

notes.front: What is the status of the Recycle reclaim policy?
notes.back: Deprecated. It performed a basic scrub (rm -rf) for reuse; dynamic provisioning is recommended instead.
notes.explanation: Only nfs and hostPath volume types support recycling.

notes.front: What is the difference between an in-tree and an out-of-tree volume plugin?
notes.back: In-tree plugins are part of the Kubernetes code and release cycle; out-of-tree plugins are developed independently.
notes.explanation: CSI is the standard way to build out-of-tree storage plugins.

notes.front: To use a storage vendor’s CSI driver, what two steps does the cluster administrator take?
notes.back: Deploy the CSI driver to the cluster, then create a StorageClass that uses it.
notes.explanation: Users then simply request that StorageClass in their PersistentVolumeClaims.

notes.front: What should replace a FlexVolume driver?
notes.back: A CSI driver.
notes.explanation: FlexVolume is deprecated; CSI addresses its limitations, such as needing driver binaries and root access on every host.

notes.front: What do the Kubernetes docs say about using hostPath volumes?
notes.back: They present many security risks; avoid them where possible, for example by using a local PersistentVolume instead.
notes.explanation: A hostPath mount exposes the node’s own filesystem to the Pod; the docs call it a powerful escape hatch that most Pods do not need.

notes.front: Which of these can be a source of a projected volume: a Secret, a ConfigMap, a ServiceAccount token?
notes.back: All three (downward API data can be projected too).
notes.explanation: A projected volume combines such sources into one directory; they must be in the Pod’s namespace.

notes.front: Is each of these stateful or stateless: (a) a shopping-basket service, (b) a service that resizes an uploaded image and returns it?
notes.back: (a) Stateful: it must remember baskets. (b) Stateless: each request stands alone.
notes.explanation: State is any data an app must store to work as designed; stateful apps need storage reachable wherever they run.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary, “Stateful Apps” and “Stateless Apps”

notes.front: A container writes its working files to its own filesystem. It crashes, the kubelet restarts it, and the files are gone. What should the Pod use to keep them across restarts?
notes.back: A volume mounted into the container.
notes.explanation: A restarted container starts with a clean filesystem; data in any kind of volume survives container restarts.

notes.front: Two containers in one Pod need shared scratch space for a large sort. The data is worthless once the Pod finishes. Which volume fits?
notes.back: A) emptyDir.
notes.choices:
A) emptyDir
B) A PersistentVolumeClaim bound to a PersistentVolume
C) hostPath
notes.choicesExplained: B keeps data beyond the Pod, which is not needed here. C exposes the node’s filesystem and carries security risks.
notes.explanation: emptyDir is created empty for the Pod, shared by its containers, and deleted with it.

notes.front: A database Pod may be deleted and rescheduled on another node, and its data must survive. Which volume fits?
notes.back: B) A PersistentVolumeClaim bound to a PersistentVolume.
notes.choices:
A) emptyDir
B) A PersistentVolumeClaim bound to a PersistentVolume
C) hostPath
notes.choicesExplained: A is deleted when the Pod leaves the node. C ties data to one node’s disk and is a security risk.
notes.explanation: PVs exist beyond the lifetime of any Pod, and the replacement Pod can mount the same claim.

notes.front: A Pod gets its settings from a configMap volume. When the Pod is deleted, what happens to that volume?
notes.back: It is destroyed with the Pod: configMap volumes are ephemeral.
notes.explanation: Ephemeral volumes follow the Pod’s lifetime; the ConfigMap object itself is unaffected.

notes.front: The only PersistentVolumes are 50Gi, dynamic provisioning is not set up, and a user creates a PVC for 100Gi. What happens?
notes.back: The claim stays unbound until a PV of at least 100Gi is added.
notes.explanation: Claims remain unbound indefinitely without a matching volume, and bind when one becomes available.

notes.front: Developers keep waiting for admins to create disks and PVs by hand. What removes the wait?
notes.back: Dynamic provisioning: admins define StorageClasses, and volumes are created automatically when developers create claims.
notes.explanation: It removes the need to pre-provision storage while still letting users choose among storage options.

notes.front: A cluster offers “fast” SSD and “slow” HDD storage. How does a user get SSD storage for their app?
notes.back: Set storageClassName: fast in the PersistentVolumeClaim.
notes.explanation: Users request a particular class by the StorageClass object’s name.

notes.front: Web Pods spread over several nodes must all write uploaded files to the same volume. Which access mode is needed?
notes.back: C) ReadWriteMany.
notes.choices:
A) ReadWriteOnce
B) ReadOnlyMany
C) ReadWriteMany
D) ReadWriteOncePod
notes.choicesExplained: A and D limit writing to one node or one Pod. B allows many nodes but read-only.
notes.explanation: Only ReadWriteMany gives read-write access from many nodes, and the storage must support it.

notes.front: You must guarantee that only one Pod in the whole cluster can read or write a claim. Which access mode?
notes.back: D) ReadWriteOncePod.
notes.choices:
A) ReadWriteOnce
B) ReadOnlyMany
C) ReadWriteMany
D) ReadWriteOncePod
notes.choicesExplained: A still lets several Pods on the same node use the volume. B and C allow many nodes.
notes.explanation: ReadWriteOncePod restricts the volume to one Pod; it needs CSI volumes.

notes.front: Deleting a PVC by mistake must never destroy the underlying disk, so an admin can recover the data. Which reclaim policy should the PV have?
notes.back: Retain.
notes.explanation: Retain keeps the PV and its data as “released” for manual reclamation; Delete would remove the storage asset too.

notes.front: A storage vendor wants its product usable in Kubernetes without adding code to the Kubernetes repository. What should it build?
notes.back: A CSI driver.
notes.explanation: CSI lets vendors create out-of-tree storage plugins that clusters install separately.

notes.front: In a review, you find an ordinary web app whose Pod mounts the node’s /etc directory with hostPath. What should you recommend?
notes.back: Remove the hostPath mount: it presents many security risks and ordinary Pods do not need it.
notes.explanation: If node-local storage is truly needed, the docs suggest a local PersistentVolume instead.

notes.front: A storage platform is designed to provide persistent data to containerised databases on Kubernetes. What category of technology is it?
notes.back: Cloud native storage.
notes.explanation: Cloud native storage is tailored to containerised environments and mainly serves stateful apps.

notes.front: What is the difference between a PersistentVolume and a PersistentVolumeClaim?
notes.back: The PV is the storage itself, a cluster resource; the PVC is a user’s request for storage that binds to a PV.
notes.explanation: Compare nodes and Pods: Pods consume node resources, PVCs consume PV resources.

notes.front: When a Pod ceases to exist, what happens to its ephemeral volumes and to its persistent volumes?
notes.back: Kubernetes destroys the ephemeral volumes but not the persistent ones.
notes.explanation: In both cases data is preserved across container restarts while the Pod exists.

notes.front: After a claim is deleted, what is the difference between the Retain and Delete reclaim policies?
notes.back: Retain keeps the PV and its data for manual cleanup; Delete removes the PV and the external storage asset.
notes.explanation: Dynamically provisioned volumes default to Delete, so set Retain on the StorageClass where data must be kept.

notes.front: What is the difference between ReadWriteOnce and ReadWriteOncePod?
notes.back: ReadWriteOnce limits read-write access to one node, which may run several Pods; ReadWriteOncePod limits it to one Pod.
notes.explanation: ReadWriteOncePod is stable since v1.29 and supported only for CSI volumes.

notes.front: Both emptyDir and hostPath use storage on the node. What is the key difference?
notes.back: emptyDir is a fresh, Pod-private directory deleted with the Pod; hostPath exposes an existing part of the node’s own filesystem.
notes.explanation: That exposure is why hostPath carries many security risks while emptyDir is ordinary scratch space.
